## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhojājānīyajātaka* (Ja 23) is a canonical birth story preserved in the *Jātaka* collection of the Pali Tipiṭaka. Set at Jetavana, the story was delivered by the Buddha concerning a monk who had abandoned his striving or persevering effort (*ossattha-viriya*) [Fausböll 1877; Readings from the Jatakas]. To encourage him, the Buddha recounted a deed of the distant past showing how the wise of old persevered and refused to give up even when wounded under adverse circumstances [Fausböll 1877].

In the narrative of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as a noble thoroughbred warhorse (*bhojājānīyasindhava*) [Fausböll 1877]. The core verse of the Jātaka (*Api passena semāno...*) records the horse urging his charioteer to harness him back into service, proclaiming that even when pierced with arrows and lying on his side, a noble destrier is superior to an ordinary steed or hack (*vaḷavā*) [Fausböll 1877]. In the resolution of the story (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identified the figures of the past: the king was Ānanda, the horse-rider (*assāroha*) was Sāriputta, and the noble destrier was the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1877]. Beyond textual transmission, the story of the Buddha in the form of this horse is visually attested in Buddhist art, including an engraved stone slab at Wat Si Chum in Sukhothai, Thailand [Boisselier 1994].
